title: Ankara-Baghdad Sign Historic Oil Transport Deal as Turkish Petroleum Takes Kirkuk Stake, Fidan Shuttles Libya Amid Haftar Intel Chief Assassination
subhead: Turkey and Iraq locked in a one-year crude transport agreement and a Turkish Petroleum stake in Kirkuk, opening a path to 1 million barrels a day of Iraqi oil as Hormuz stays choked. In Libya, Fidan's two-day shuttle of Tripoli and Benghazi collided with the assassination of the LNA's intelligence chief, testing Ankara's 'One Libya' balancing act.

sections.heading: Ankara-Baghdad Energy Deal: Kirkuk Equity and a 1M bpd Ambition
sections.body:
Turkey and Iraq signed a one-year 'Crude Oil Transport Agreement' in Ankara, negotiated between BOTAŞ and Iraq's SOMO and North Oil Company (NOC), allocating 750,000 barrels per day of pipeline capacity to Iraq's state oil firms on the Silopi-Ceyhan system, according to Azernews. Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar called it 'a historic agreement,' adding that Turkish Petroleum becoming a partner in the Kirkuk oil fields was a truly historic and vital milestone.'

Bayraktar said the initiative raised during President Erdogan's meeting with Iraqi PM Ali al-Zaidi for Iraq to supply 1 million barrels per day of crude to Turkish refineries is 'genuinely crucial for our country's oil supply security.' He also floated the ambition of moving oil from Iraq — and 'perhaps in the future from Kuwait and other Gulf nations' — through Ceyhan to global markets, bypassing the choked Strait of Hormuz.
sections.whyItMatters: This converts Turkey's energy security from a Gulf-dependent posture into a land-bridge strategy. With Hormuz gridlocked and oil above $90, the Ceyhan corridor — and Turkish Petroleum's equity in Kirkuk — gives Ankara a hedge against Gulf disruption and a stronger hand in regional energy politics.

sections.heading: Fidan Shuttles Tripoli and Benghazi as Haftar's Intel Chief Is Killed
sections.body:
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan completed a two-day Libya visit (Aug 11-12), meeting PM Abdulhamid Dbeibeh in Tripoli and then General Saddam Haftar, deputy commander of the Libyan National Army, in Benghazi, per ILKHA. Ankara frames the outreach as a 'One Libya' policy supporting a unified country rather than treating east and west as permanent rivals.

The shuttle unfolded against a violent backdrop: Maj. Gen. Fawzi al-Mansouri, head of military intelligence for the eastern-based LNA, was assassinated in a car bombing in Benghazi on Monday as he left a mosque, according to Anadolu Agency and France 24. Analysts cited by MSN said the killing was a major blow to the Haftar family's security credentials and could delay a US-brokered plan to reunify Libya's rival governments. Tripoli's government condemned the killing as a 'terrorist act' and urged a probe.
sections.whyItMatters: Fidan's dual-track diplomacy shows Ankara hedging across Libya's divide even as it deepens ties with the east. But Mansouri's assassination — in an LNA stronghold — exposes the fragility of the security environment Ankara is betting on, and could complicate the US-led unification push Turkey is trying to stay ahead of.

sections.heading: Oil Dips Below $90 as Hormuz Deadlock Persists
sections.body:
Crude prices fell more than $1 on Thursday, dipping below $90, as forecasters cut 2026 global demand projections, Reuters reported. The OPEC monthly report lowered its 2026 demand-growth forecast to 580,000 barrels per day, and the IEA also trimmed its outlook, citing demand destruction from the US-Iran war and Hormuz disruption.

For Turkey, the price relief is modest: the country remains exposed to elevated energy import costs, and the Iraq deal is a medium-term hedge rather than an immediate fix. The US-Iran pause for diplomacy continues, but Iran has claimed control of the Strait and said it is not seeking talks, per global headlines.
sections.whyItMatters: Lower demand forecasts are easing the oil shock that has pressured Turkey's import bill, but the Hormuz impasse keeps the risk premium alive. Ankara's push for Iraqi and Gulf crude via Ceyhan is a direct strategic response to this prolonged supply uncertainty.

sections.heading: PKK Peace Law Enters Force, Implementation Questions Loom
sections.body:
Turkey's conditional pardon law for thousands of PKK militants is now in force after parliament passed it this week, linking legal relief to verified disarmament, per Reuters and AP. The law, the first legislation to emerge from direct negotiations with jailed PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan, offers a path to ending a conflict that has killed tens of thousands.

Implementation remains the open question. PKK leaders say deeper reforms and Ocalan's role remain unresolved, and the law's near-unanimous passage reflects the ruling elite closing ranks rather than a settled peace, as the WSWS noted. The process now hinges on whether militants actually disarm and how the state verifies it.
sections.whyItMatters: The law is on the books, but the hard part — verified disarmament and the political status of Ocalan — is ahead. How Ankara sequences implementation will determine whether this is a genuine peace opening or a controlled legal framework that leaves the core disputes unresolved.

sections.heading: Economy: Inflation Eases to 31.75% as Rate Holds at 37%
sections.body:
Turkey's official July CPI inflation eased to 31.75% year-on-year, down from 32.11% in June, per TurkStat data reported by MSN. The central bank has held its key rate at 37% for a third consecutive meeting, monitoring the inflation impact of the Iran war, Reuters reported in June.

No major new policy move was announced today. The easing inflation trend is welcome, but Turkish businesses continue to complain about high interest rates and limited credit access, with bank profits drying up, per a Financial Times-style report in MSN.
sections.whyItMatters: Disinflation is proceeding, but the 37% policy rate keeps credit tight and growth constrained. The central bank's caution reflects the tension between taming prices and the energy-cost shock from the regional war — a balance that will define Turkey's economic trajectory through the rest of 2026.

bottomLine: Today's defining development is Turkey's energy pivot: a historic BOTAŞ-SOMO transport deal, Turkish Petroleum's equity stake in Kirkuk, and a 1 million bpd Iraqi supply ambition that positions Ceyhan as a land-based alternative to the choked Strait of Hormuz. In Libya, Fidan's dual-track shuttle of Tripoli and Benghazi ran into the assassination of the LNA's intelligence chief — a reminder that the unification push Ankara is trying to shape remains fragile. The PKK peace law is now law, but implementation and Ocalan's status will test it. With oil easing below $90 and inflation at 31.75%, Turkey's near-term economic pressure is moderating, but the strategic bets on Iraqi crude and Libyan stability carry the real long-term stakes.
sources: Azernews, ILKHA, Anadolu Agency, France 24, Reuters, MSN, AP, Forbes, WSWS, OPEC monthly report, IEA
